name: Class A
tagline: The jet highway — IFR only, always
shape: Covers the entire contiguous U.S., Alaska, Hawaii, and overlying U.S. airspace nationwide.
description: Class A is the highest controlled airspace, used exclusively for IFR operations. All jets and turboprops cruise here under positive ATC control. VFR flight is completely prohibited. You'll be talking to Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs) the entire time.

dimensions.horizontal: Contiguous U.S., Alaska, Hawaii, and overlying international airspace

clearance_details: ATC IFR clearance required before entering. VFR operations are not permitted under any circumstances. File and activate an IFR flight plan before departure.
two_way_comm: Required — maintained with ATC throughout the flight (ARTCCs)

weather_minimums.note: IFR only — VFR weather minimums do not apply.

entry_requirements.req: File and activate an IFR flight plan
Obtain ATC IFR clearance prior to entry
Instrument rating (required pilot certificate)
IFR-equipped aircraft
Transponder with Mode C operating
Two-way radio contact with ARTCC throughout

fun_fact: Above 18,000 MSL, all altimeters are set to 29.92 in Hg (standard pressure). You no longer say '25,000 feet' — you say 'Flight Level 250.' This eliminates altimeter setting errors that could cause altitude conflicts between aircraft.

name: Class B
tagline: Upside-down wedding cake — get that clearance
shape: Upside-down wedding cake: multiple concentric circular tiers, each with a higher floor as you move outward. Centered on the primary airport at major hubs (LAX, JFK, ORD, ATL, DFW).
description: Class B surrounds the nation's busiest commercial airports. The tiered shape allows aircraft to transition underneath it. The key rule: you must hear the explicit words 'cleared into Class Bravo' — nothing else qualifies as entry clearance.

dimensions.floor: Surface at the primary airport, rising in steps outward
dimensions.ceiling: Typically 10,000 ft MSL (varies per individual airport)
dimensions.horizontal: Typically 10–30 nm radius in tiered rings. A 30 nm Mode C Veil extends beyond the boundary.

clearance_details: Explicit ATC clearance required — you must hear 'cleared into Class Bravo.' A response of 'N12345, standby' does NOT grant permission to enter. You must receive and read back the full clearance.
two_way_comm: Required before and throughout operations within Class B
transponder: Mode C required inside Class B and within the entire 30 nm Mode C Veil of the primary airport
pilot_certificate: Private Pilot certificate minimum. Student pilots require a specific instructor endorsement for that Class B airport.
aircraft_equipment: Transponder with Mode C (within B and 30 nm veil)

weather_minimums.note: Unique to Class B: no specific cloud distance requirement.

entry_requirements.req: Private Pilot certificate (or student with a specific Class B endorsement)
Explicit ATC clearance — must hear 'cleared into Class Bravo'
Transponder with Mode C operating
ADS-B Out equipment
3 SM visibility and clear of clouds (VFR)

fun_fact: The 30 nm Mode C Veil extends well beyond the charted Class B boundary. If you're within 30 nm of a Class B primary airport, you need a Mode C transponder — even if you never enter the B itself. This surprises many student pilots near large cities.

name: Class C
tagline: Talk before you enter — two-way comm is enough
shape: Two concentric circles: inner 5 nm ring (surface to 4,000 AGL) and outer 5–10 nm ring (1,200 AGL to 4,000 AGL). Depicted with solid magenta rings on sectional charts.
description: Class C surrounds airports with an operational TRACON (Terminal Radar Approach Control). You don't need explicit clearance — just establish two-way communication with approach control before entering. But ATC must acknowledge your specific callsign, not just 'aircraft calling.'

dimensions.ceiling: ~4,000 ft AGL above the primary airport elevation
dimensions.horizontal: 5 nm inner ring, 10 nm outer ring, plus an informal ~20 nm outer area (voluntary services)

clearance_details: No explicit clearance needed — establish two-way communication before entering. CRITICAL: ATC must acknowledge your specific callsign. 'Aircraft calling, standby' (without your tail number) does NOT establish two-way comm. Wait until they use your N-number.
two_way_comm: Must be established prior to entry — ATC must acknowledge your specific callsign
transponder: Mode C required within Class C and within 10 nm of the primary airport up to 10,000 MSL
pilot_certificate: No special certification required — student pilot OK

weather_minimums.cloud_clearance: 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal

entry_requirements.req: Establish two-way comm with approach control — ATC must use your callsign
Transponder with Mode C operating
ADS-B Out equipment
3 SM visibility, 500/1,000/2,000 cloud clearance

fun_fact: Class C has an outer area extending to about 20 nm that isn't depicted on charts. ATC services are available there but participation is voluntary — you can opt in for radar advisories. Only within the two solid magenta rings is communication mandatory.

name: Class D
tagline: Towered airport — say hello before you enter
shape: Roughly circular, ~4–5 nm radius around a towered airport. Depicted with a dashed blue circle on sectional charts. Ceiling shown as [XX] in hundreds of feet MSL (e.g., [25] = 2,500 AGL).
description: Class D surrounds airports with an operational control tower but no radar approach control. Entry is simple: talk to the tower before crossing the boundary. When the tower closes (part-time towers), Class D ceases to exist and reverts to Class E or G.

dimensions.ceiling: ~2,500 ft AGL (shown on sectional as [XX] in hundreds of feet MSL)
dimensions.horizontal: Typically 4–5 nm radius, dashed blue circle on sectional charts

clearance_details: No clearance required — just establish two-way communication with the tower before entering. Same callsign rule as Class C: ATC must acknowledge your specific tail number.
two_way_comm: Must be established prior to entry — ATC must acknowledge your callsign
transponder: Not specifically required for Class D — required only if overlying airspace (B, C, or Mode C Veil) mandates it
pilot_certificate: No special certification required — student pilot OK
aircraft_equipment: Transponder if required by overlying airspace

weather_minimums.cloud_clearance: 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal

entry_requirements.req: Establish two-way radio communication with the control tower before entry
3 SM visibility, 500/1,000/2,000 from clouds

fun_fact: Always check tower hours. Part-time towers are common, and when the tower closes, Class D airspace ceases to exist. Check the Chart Supplement or sectional for tower operating hours — it completely changes your communication requirements after hours.

name: Class E
tagline: IFR protected, VFR free — the great middle layer
shape: Everything controlled that isn't A, B, C, or D. Exists nationwide at various floors: surface at some non-towered airports, 700 AGL (magenta vignette), 1,200 AGL (en-route), or 14,500 MSL in remote areas.
description: Class E is the most common airspace in the country. Its primary purpose is to protect IFR traffic on airways and approaches. VFR pilots can fly through it freely without talking to anyone. The floor varies by location — reading sectional charts is key.

dimensions.floor: Varies: surface (some airports) / 700 AGL (magenta vignette) / 1,200 AGL (typical) / 14,500 MSL (remote areas)
dimensions.ceiling: 17,999 ft MSL (the floor of Class A at 18,000)
dimensions.horizontal: Nationwide everywhere not covered by other classes, plus overlying domestic oceanic airspace

clearance_details: VFR pilots need no clearance and no communication with ATC. IFR flights require ATC clearance (as always for IFR).
two_way_comm: Not required for VFR flight. IFR flights must maintain ATC contact.
transponder: Mode C required above 10,000 MSL (except within 2,500 AGL of terrain). Also required in Mode C Veil areas.
pilot_certificate: No special certification required — student pilot OK
aircraft_equipment: Transponder with Mode C above 10,000 MSL
ADS-B Out above 10,000 MSL and in designated Class E airspace at airports

weather_minimums.note: Different minimums above and below 10,000 MSL.

below_10000.cloud_clearance: 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal

above_10000.cloud_clearance: 1,000 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 1 SM horizontal

entry_requirements.req: No specific entry requirements for VFR flight
Meet VFR weather minimums for the altitude
Mode C transponder required above 10,000 MSL
ADS-B Out required above 10,000 MSL (and other designated areas)

fun_fact: A magenta vignette (fading border) on a sectional means Class E starts at 700 AGL — it protects instrument approaches. A solid blue border means 1,200 AGL. No vignette at all? Class G all the way up until the en-route E structure begins.

name: Class G
tagline: Uncontrolled — fly free, see and avoid
altRange: Surface to Class E floor (~0–1,200 AGL)
shape: Everything that isn't A, B, C, D, or E. Typically the lowest-altitude airspace — 0 to 1,200 AGL in most rural areas, 0 to 700 AGL near instrument approach airports. No chart designation — you identify it by elimination.
description: Class G is completely uncontrolled airspace. ATC provides no separation services here. No clearance, no communication, no transponder required. Most low-altitude rural flying happens here. Just meet the weather minimums — which are the most permissive of any airspace.

dimensions.ceiling: The floor of Class E above (typically 700 or 1,200 AGL; up to 14,500 MSL in remote western areas)
dimensions.horizontal: Everywhere below the floor of Class E — primarily rural and remote areas

clearance_details: No clearance required. No ATC contact required. This is truly uncontrolled airspace — see and avoid applies fully. Simply meet the weather minimums.
transponder: Not specifically required (unless within a Mode C Veil or other airspace requiring one)
pilot_certificate: Student pilot OK (with appropriate solo endorsements)
aircraft_equipment: No specific equipment requirements for VFR flight

weather_minimums.note: Most permissive minimums in the NAS — vary by altitude and day/night.

night_below_1200_agl.cloud_clearance: 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal

day_1200_to_10000.cloud_clearance: 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal

night_1200_to_10000.cloud_clearance: 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal

above_10000.cloud_clearance: 1,000 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 1 SM horizontal

entry_requirements.req: No communication, clearance, or transponder required (check for Mode C Veil exceptions)
Day, < 1,200 AGL: 1 SM visibility, clear of clouds
Night, < 1,200 AGL: 3 SM visibility, 500/1,000/2,000 from clouds

fun_fact: Class G isn't 'designated' anywhere — it's defined as what remains after all other classes are removed. You won't find a single 'G' label on any sectional chart. You identify it purely by process of elimination: if nothing else covers it, it's G.
